chapter: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
title: Ear training and music as inborn
summary: Thompson argues that music is born in you and needs an ear for tempo and timing; money helps you improve it.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: And so as I said, I had learned, being around these other musicians and listening, which is one of the secrets of playing most any kind of music, as we talked about before, the ear. The ear training. Because no matter how much music one might study, they could study forever and ever and a day, you know. If they didn't have an ear for music, and a perfect understanding of tempo and timing, they'll

never make a professional musician. And this is one of the sad parts of many people send their children to school to become musicians, spend a lot of money giving them lessons, and some even insist and use violence to force their children to be musicians, hoping they'll be great. It's just not -- it's born in you.

Yes, it is. There's no doubt in my mind that music is born in you and what is given you you have to improve on with your knowledge and study. Now as I said before your economical situation has to do with how much you can improve it and how fast you can improve by the help of others, by teachers and so forth and so on. And I think this is a guideline of what jazz music is all about, which I'd like to in some way give some ideas about so the people could really understand jazz music better. Because I think that many people, because they don't understand what jazz is about, even though they may not feel it, if they really understood what it was about they might have a better appreciation for it.
